extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law / political science
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the principles, institutional norms, and practical restraints that govern the behaviour and authority of the United States Federal (Supreme) courts. Includes discussion of non-justiciability, precedent, judicial independence, professional norms, and practical problems (delay, caseload).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-interference in purely political questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme court — has always declared that it is not concerned with purely political questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotational guidance: 'In measures exclusively of a political, legislative, or executive character ... the supreme authority as to these questions belongs to the legislative and executive departments, they cannot be re-examined elsewhere.' Examples: declarations that war-making, taxation, appropriations, treaty-making and their modes of execution are beyond re-examination by courts; remedy for political abuses is appeal to the people or constitutional amendment. Anti-pattern: courts re-examining inherently political policy judgments rather than legal questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for discretion accorded to executive and legislative actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it finds any discretion given to the President, any executive duty imposed on him, it considers the manner in which he exercises his discretion and discharges the duty to be beyond its province; when the Constitution confers upon Congress a power of legislating, the court declines to inquire whether the use of the power was in a particular statute either necessary or desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: courts should distinguish legal questions from policy/discretionary judgments of political branches and refrain from substituting judicial views of prudence or desirability for those branches. Example/anti-pattern: treating legislative prudence as justiciable and substituting court judgment for Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to decide abstract questions or give advisory opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking upon itself as a pure organ of the law, commissioned to do justice between man and man, the Supreme court has steadily refused to decide abstract questions, or to give opinions in advance by way of advice to the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: declined Washington's 1793 request for opinion on treaty construction. Stated drawbacks of refusing advisory opinions: uncertainty about when a constitutional point will be settled; expense and reluctance of parties to litigate; late decisions can upset private interests that relied on prior understandings. Trade-off: refusal preserves judicial role but can delay needed clarifying rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of immersion in party politics to maintain dignity and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges, when sucked into the vortex of politics, must lose dignity, impartiality, and influence. Adherence to the principle of non-interference has enabled the court to avoid an immixture in political strife which must have destroyed its credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes that sustain this norm: judicial restraint on political questions, professional feeling among lawyers, the bench-bar relation, security of tenure. Anti-patterns: judicial behaviour that openly pursues party objectives or acts as a partisan organ (examples: Dred Scott's political effects; electoral-count involvement of 1877).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence through security of tenure and irremovability
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a judge is irremovable (except by impeachment), he has nothing to fear from party displeasure, nothing to hope from party favour; this external condition favors virtue and independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: secure tenure encourages capable men to accept judgeships and reduces incentive to conciliate parties for reappointment. Practical caveat: appointment is political, but incumbents generally 'leave partisanship behind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the bar and professional norms as a restraining/legitimizing influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The keen interest which the profession takes in the law secures a large number of acute and competent critics of the interpretation put upon the law by the judges. Such men form a tribunal to whose opinion the judges are sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: judges' prior practice as counsel, sympathy with the bar, and desire for professional approbation help keep them from prostituting office to party objects. Example: returning advocates welcomed by their local bar; professional criticism assists public acceptance of court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of law vs. correcting bad precedent (stare decisis balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court has not always followed its own former decisions. It must choose between the evil of unsettling the law by reversing, and the evil of perpetuating bad law by following a former decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: because only a constitutional amendment can change constitutional law, the court may sometimes reasonably reverse prior decisions in extreme cases. Anti-pattern: frequent reversals that unsettle reliance; but rigid adherence can perpetuate serious error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court as the living voice of the Constitution and guarantor of minority rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme court is the living voice of the Constitution ... the guarantee of the minority, who, when threatened by the impatient vehemence of a majority, can appeal to this permanent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: to fulfill this function the court must be stable, resist transitory impulses and popular sentiment, and be able to defy both attacks from other departments and seductive popular pressure. This is normative guidance on the court's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality, integrity, and avoidance of corruption or overt partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: No one of its members has ever been suspected of corruption, and comparatively few have allowed their political sympathies to disturb their official judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the reputation for probity underpins judicial authority; appointment practices should aim to secure men of character. Anti-patterns: appointments or actions that create plausible perceptions of corruption or partisanship (e.g., appointments seen as altering the court’s view on a question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acting in non-judicial capacities (avoid extra-constitutional functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function scarcely judicial, and certainly not contemplated by the Constitution, was then for the first time thrown upon the judiciary [electoral commission of 1877], and in discharging it the judiciary acted exactly like non-judicial persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: courts should avoid taking on roles not envisaged by constitutional design; doing so risks voting on party lines and damaging legitimacy. Anti-pattern: participating in political commissions or counts that demand political rather than judicial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of capable and eminent judges to secure authority
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not call that a result of fortune which was the result of the wisdom of successive Presidents in choosing capable men to sit on the supreme Federal bench. John Marshall ... rendered such incomparable services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: appointing judges of high ability and reputation builds the court's moral authority and public esteem; individual eminence can form lasting traditions that guide successors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage caseloads and timeliness to preserve legal certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrears have so accumulated that it is sometimes three years or more from the time when a cause is entered till the day when it comes on for hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested remedies: limit right of appeal to cases involving a considerable sum of money; divide the Supreme court into divisional courts for ordinary suits while reserving full court for constitutional points. Guidance highlights the practical need for institutional reforms to avoid long delays that unsettle expectations and law.
